cls: Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitor - topical ocular antiglaucoma agent
pharm: A Rho-associated protein kinase inhibitor given as an ophthalmic solution that lowers intraocular pressure primarily by increasing aqueous humor outflow through the trabecular meshwork (and reducing episcleral venous pressure), used in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension.
quick: One drop in the affected eye(s) once daily in the evening
Not applicable - topical ophthalmic; no food interaction

summary: Netarsudil ophthalmic solution 0.02% (Rhopressa) is a Rho kinase inhibitor indicated to reduce elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in patients with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension. The dose is one drop in the affected eye(s) once daily in the evening; twice-daily dosing is not recommended because it is less effective and may be less well tolerated. The most common adverse effect is conjunctival hyperemia (about half of patients); corneal verticillata (whorl-like deposits) and conjunctival hemorrhage are also common. Systemic absorption is minimal. Contact lenses must be removed before instillation and may be reinserted 15 minutes later.
indications: Reduction of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in patients with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension

dosage.d: One drop in the affected eye(s) once daily in the evening
dosage.n: Twice-daily dosing is NOT recommended (less effective, poorer tolerability)

dosage.d: Resume with the next scheduled evening dose

dosage.c: Use with other topical eye drops
dosage.d: Separate administration of different eye drops by at least 5 minutes

admin: Instill one drop in the evening; consistent evening dosing optimizes IOP control
Wash hands; do not touch the dropper tip to the eye or any surface to avoid contamination
If using other topical ophthalmic products, administer them at least 5 minutes apart
Remove contact lenses before instillation (contains benzalkonium chloride); reinsert 15 minutes after dosing
Apply gentle nasolacrimal occlusion (press inner corner of eye) after instilling to minimize systemic absorption
moa: Netarsudil is an inhibitor of Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK). The exact mechanism by which it lowers intraocular pressure is not fully established but is believed to involve increasing the outflow of aqueous humor through the trabecular (conventional) meshwork - the principal route of drainage - by relaxing the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal cells. It also lowers episcleral venous pressure. Its active metabolite (netarsudil-M1) is also a ROCK inhibitor and additionally inhibits the norepinephrine transporter.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to netarsudil or any component of the formulation
relative: Pre-existing corneal stromal edema (risk of corneal epithelial edema/honeycomb pattern)
Contact lens wearers (remove lenses before use due to benzalkonium chloride)
monitor: Cornea for verticillata (whorl deposits) and corneal/epithelial edema
Signs of ocular infection (avoid contaminating the dropper tip)

preg: There are no available human data to inform drug-associated risk during pregnancy. Systemic exposure following topical ocular administration is minimal, so fetal risk is expected to be low. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: There are no data on the presence of netarsudil in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant. Because systemic exposure after ophthalmic dosing is low, clinically relevant exposure of the breastfed infant is not expected; breastfeeding is generally considered compatible.
renal: No dose adjustment is necessary. Systemic absorption after topical ocular administration is negligible, so renal impairment is not expected to affect therapy.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is necessary. Systemic absorption after topical ocular administration is negligible, so hepatic impairment is not expected to affect therapy.

minor: Other topical ophthalmic medications - separate instillation by at least 5 minutes to avoid washout
interactions.diagnostics: May produce visible whorl-like corneal deposits (verticillata) on slit-lamp examination, which resolve after discontinuation.

serious: Corneal epithelial edema (honeycomb or bullous, in pre-existing stromal edema)
rare: Lacrimation increase, eye irritation, dry eye
emergency: Bacterial keratitis with eye pain, discharge, and decreased vision (seek prompt ophthalmologic care)

monitoring: Slit-lamp examination for corneal verticillata and corneal/epithelial edema
Signs of ocular infection or hypersensitivity
counsel: Use one drop in the evening every day, even if you feel fine - glaucoma usually has no symptoms
Do not let the bottle tip touch your eye or anything else, to avoid infection
Red eyes are common with this medicine and are usually harmless
If you wear contact lenses, take them out before using the drop and wait 15 minutes before putting them back in
If you use other eye drops, wait at least 5 minutes between them
Tell your eye doctor about eye pain, sudden vision changes, or thick discharge
pk: IOP reduction within hours; near-maximal effect over days to weeks
Plasma levels very low/negligible after ocular dosing
Local ocular effect supports once-daily dosing; systemic exposure minimal
Once-daily dosing maintains IOP control over 24 hours
Store at 2-8 C until opened; after opening may be kept at 2-25 C for up to 6 weeks
pearls: ROCK inhibitor - lowers IOP by improving trabecular meshwork outflow and reducing episcleral venous pressure
Dose ONCE daily in the EVENING; twice-daily is less effective and less tolerated
Conjunctival hyperemia (redness) is the most common adverse effect - counsel patients in advance
Corneal verticillata (whorl deposits) appear around 4 weeks and resolve after stopping; usually no vision effect
Refrigerate unopened; once opened, room-temperature storage up to 6 weeks
A complementary outflow mechanism makes it useful as add-on to prostaglandin analogs (e.g., fixed combination with latanoprost)
missed: If you miss your evening dose, skip it and continue with your next scheduled evening dose. Do not use extra drops to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Topical ocular overdose is not expected to cause significant harm because of negligible systemic absorption; excess drops can be flushed from the eye with lukewarm water. Accidental ingestion is unlikely to produce serious systemic toxicity; manage supportively and contact a poison control center if a large quantity is swallowed.
